adjudication_records.issue_text: [75][P1] app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/group/members.hbs:6 — `{{#each m in members}}` — setupController supplies the Group only as `model`, so the unqualified `members` property is absent and the public members table cannot render the fetched list.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff for group-members.js.es6 route, the setupController sets `controller.set("model", model)` where model is the Group object, then calls `model.findMembers()`. In the Group model's findMembers method, it sets `members` as a property on the group itself via `self.setProperties({...members: result.members.map(...)})`. So the Group object (which is the model) will have a `members` property after findMembers() completes. In the template group/members.hbs, `{{#each m in members}}` would look for `members` on the controller's context. Since the controller's model is the Group, and the Group has `members` set on it, the template should be able to access `model.members` or just `members` if the controller proxies to the model. However, the template uses `{{#each m in members}}` without `model.` prefix. In Ember, if the controller doesn't have a `members` property directly, it would need to be `model.members`. The finding appears valid - the template references `members` directly but the controller only has `model` set, and `members` is a property on the model, not the controller.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [75][P1] app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb:90 — `group.users.delete(user_id)` — the association deletion API takes user records or a relation, so this coerced integer can raise instead of removing the selected user.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, line 90 in app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb shows `group.users.delete(user_id)` where `user_id = params.require(:user_id).to_i`. The ActiveRecord `delete` method on a has_many association can accept an integer ID directly - it will find and delete the association record with that ID. However, the finding claims this 'can raise instead of removing the selected user'. In Rails, `collection.delete(id)` on a has_many :through or has_and_belongs_to_many association does work with integer IDs. The `delete` method accepts records or IDs. Looking at Rails documentation, `delete(*records)` can take 'records' which can be objects or IDs. So this should work correctly. The finding appears to be incorrect about the API behavior - Rails associations' delete method does accept integer IDs.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [100][P1] app/controllers/groups_controller.rb:22 — `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` — public groups over 50 members are silently truncated because the changed members template has no pagination controls.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the public groups/members.hbs template at line 'app/assets/javascripts/discourse/templates/group/members.hbs' shows it iterates over 'members' but has no pagination controls added. The admin group template does have pagination (previous/next buttons with currentPage/totalPages), but the public-facing group members template only has the table structure without any pagination UI. The controller now enforces a limit of 50 by default, and while the model has pagination properties (limit, offset, user_count), the public template doesn't expose any way to navigate pages. This means groups with more than 50 members will only show the first 50 with no way for users to see the rest.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [100][P1] app/controllers/groups_controller.rb:28 — `render json: { members: serialize_data(members, GroupUserSerializer), meta: { ... } }` — changing the established public members endpoint from a bare array to an object envelope without versioning breaks callers that iterate the response as an array.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the members endpoint in groups_controller.rb changing from `render_serialized(members.to_a, GroupUserSerializer)` (which returns a bare array) to `render json: { members: serialize_data(...), meta: {...} }` (which returns an object with 'members' and 'meta' keys). This is indeed a breaking API change. The finding correctly identifies that the template in group/members.hbs was updated from `{{#each m in model}}` to `{{#each m in members}}` to accommodate this change. However, looking at the route in group-members.js.es6, it now calls `model.findMembers()` which updates the model's `members` property directly. The public API endpoint `/groups/:group_id/members.json` has changed its response format, which could break external callers expecting an array. This is a real backwards compatibility concern for any external API consumers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [100][P1] app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb:38 — `group.name = (params[:name] || '').strip` — replacing the `group[name]` request contract with an unwrapped parameter makes existing admin clients submit no name and create an unintended blank or invalid group.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the diff, the create method changes from `params[:group][:name]` to `params[:name]`. However, examining the JavaScript side in group.js, the `create` function sends `data: this.asJSON()` which returns `{name: this.get('name'), alias_level: this.get('alias_level'), visible: !!this.get('visible')}`. This sends parameters as top-level keys (name, alias_level, visible), not nested under 'group'. The old code expected `params[:group][:name]` but the new client code sends `params[:name]`. The controller change aligns with the new client code. The finding claims this breaks 'existing admin clients' but the diff shows both client and server are being updated together in this changeset. The new client sends unwrapped parameters and the new server expects unwrapped parameters - they are consistent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [100][P2] app/controllers/groups_controller.rb:22 — `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` — an unbounded client-controlled page size can materialize and serialize an entire large group, defeating the pagination bound.

adjudication.rationale: The code at line 22 shows `limit = (params[:limit] || 50).to_i` which allows a client to pass any arbitrary limit value. There's no upper bound check, so a malicious client could pass `limit=1000000` to retrieve and serialize all users in a group at once, bypassing the intended pagination. This is a real security/performance issue - the pagination is meant to limit data returned, but without a max limit check, it's ineffective.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [100][P2] app/assets/javascripts/admin/controllers/admin-group.js.es6:13 — `return Math.floor(this.get("user_count") / this.get("limit")) + 1;` — exact multiples advertise an extra page, whose offset equals total and renders as a valid empty page.

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the totalPages calculation on line 13: `return Math.floor(this.get("user_count") / this.get("limit")) + 1;`. With limit=50 and user_count=100, this gives Math.floor(100/50) + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 pages. But 100 users with 50 per page should only be 2 pages (page 1: users 0-49, page 2: users 50-99). The correct formula should be Math.ceil(user_count / limit) or Math.floor((user_count - 1) / limit) + 1. This is a real bug that would show an extra empty page when user_count is an exact multiple of limit.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [100][P2] app/controllers/admin/groups_controller.rb:71 — `usernames.split(",").each do |username|` — bulk membership adds make one `User.find_by_username` query per username rather than a set-based lookup.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the code at line 71 iterates through usernames and makes individual User.find_by_username queries for each one. This is indeed an N+1 query pattern - if adding 10 users, it makes 10 separate database queries instead of one batch query like User.where(username: usernames.split(',')). This is a real performance issue/inefficiency in the code that was introduced in this diff.
